## DTV v0.1.2

The first public build of a real-time speech-to-speech pipeline: microphone → ring buffer → pause-chunked ASR → punctuation normalisation → sentence splitting → streaming TTS → ordered playback. You speak, and your voice comes back out in another voice sentence by sentence while you are still talking. Two knobs decide when a sentence ends and when a whole utterance ends; everything else is machinery.

## New

### Capture and segmentation

- Fixed-rate capture at 16 kHz mono float32 in 512-sample frames, with gain applied and clipped inside the `sounddevice` callback rather than on a second thread.
- A ring buffer carrying a cumulative stream clock: a read whose cursor has already been overwritten returns `None` instead of silently handing back garbage, so the caller can resynchronise.
- Every submit ends in one of three states — `QUEUED`, `SKIPPED` (too short, the window overflowed, or under 15 % of it was voiced), `BUSY` (backlog full; the cursor is kept and the same audio is retried on the next tick, so nothing is dropped and nothing is duplicated).
- Punctuation is treated as a hint, not as truth: the model's `,;:` become `，`, and only `? ! ！ ？` plus the `。` appended at a pause survive as sentence ends. That is what keeps the TTS from chopping a sentence in the middle because the ASR emitted a comma.

### Streaming TTS and ordered playback

- `POST /tts` with `stream: true`; 24 kHz floats are reassembled on 4-byte boundaries into 100 ms chunks, so the player starts before synthesis finishes.
- Strict ordering: the player waits for `next_seq`, so one slow sentence delays the queue but can never reorder it.
- One `OutputStream` is cached per sample rate — reopening a stream per segment costs 20–240 ms and leaks the previous one.
- Every segment ends with a `final` marker, and a failed synthesis sends a zero-length tombstone, so playback cannot wait forever on a segment that will never arrive.

### Control panel and tray

- A Tkinter form mirroring the CLI, one field per option, seeded from `config.ini` plus the defaults, with device pickers and a reference-audio browse button.
- While running, `sys.stdout` / `stderr` are swapped for a queue-backed stream, so `[asr]` / `[tts]` lines land in the log pane; a level meter shows current RMS against the threshold, which is what you calibrate `silence_threshold` against.
- Saving rewrites only the affected line in `[pipeline]` — comments, other sections and CRLF endings are preserved, so a hand-edited config is never mangled by the UI.
- Minimise to tray through `Shell_NotifyIconW` on its own thread; the tray menu offers show, start/stop and quit.

### Packaging

- One PyInstaller spec, two executables in `dist/DTV/`: `DTV-gui.exe` (windowed, no console) and `DTV.exe` (console, same CLI).
- `config.ini` and `speaker.wav` are copied next to the executables after the build and never overwritten, so an upgrade keeps your settings and your reference voice.
- PortAudio and libsndfile are collected explicitly with `collect_dynamic_libs` from `_sounddevice_data` / `_soundfile_data`, which static analysis cannot follow.
- `Dockerfile.tts` is included for running the TTS side without a Windows desktop.
- The application now ships its own icon: a white rounded tile with a microphone and sound waves, transparent outside the tile.

## Notes

- Python 3.11+; needs a llama-server instance serving Qwen3-ASR-4B for recognition and a TTS endpoint for synthesis — the README's "bring up the two servers" section is the quickest path.
- Stack: numpy · sounddevice · soundfile · httpx · Tkinter · ctypes (Win32 tray) · PyInstaller · ruff.
